mappings.note: MISFILED chemistry (10SCIENCE5qa). From Z = 7, 10, 12, 4, 19 pick the chemically similar pair, the inert gas, the period-3 member and the non-metal. All four from configuration and position, C 1.1.
Periodic-table fragment: Na's look-alikes with a reason, configurations of N and P, a property shared by F and Cl. The stored answer confirms every part turns on valence-shell configuration, C 1.1.
Radii list is dropped from the printed stem, but the stored answer shows the item orders second-period radii and asks how radius changes left to right. Across-period size trend, C 1.1.
Chlorine (Z=17): configuration, valency, group, ion type and compound formula. C 1.1 covers compound formation from valency, so no separate C 1.3 citation is needed -- nothing is reacted or balanced.

Group list across a period: which table it represents, the oxygen family, the unreactive group -- all C 1.1. The last part, which groups form ionic bonds most readily, is metal/non-metal interaction, so C 1.3 is cited alongside.

The configuration itself is missing from the printed stem, but the stored answer (Z = 16, sulphur) shows all four parts are group, period, valence electrons and valency. Determinable, so mapped: C 1.1.
Last of the misfiled chemistry run. Table fragment asks for the most reactive metal, the halogen family, group 2/15/18 members and the element below carbon. Identification by position, C 1.1.

Why diffusion cannot meet a multicellular organism's oxygen need. The answer is a surface-area-to-volume argument about body organisation, which is C 4.2 (levels of organisation from molecules to organisms), not C 3.2-LO-2 -- no human organ or pathway is named, and the point holds for any large organism.
What criteria decide something is alive. This is the life-processes competency at its broadest; no LO fits because LO-1/2/3 each name a specific process, and this question deliberately refuses to.
Outside raw materials an organism uses (food, water, oxygen). Spans nutrition, respiration and transport at once, so the competency C 3.2 rather than any single LO.
Which processes are essential for maintaining life -- names the whole set of life processes, so the competency, not one of its LOs.
Differences between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition -- this is the literal first clause of C 3.2-LO-1.

Where a plant gets each raw material for photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is the autotrophic half of C 3.2-LO-1; C 3.1 is not cited because the question is about sources of CO2, water and minerals, not about the chloroplast.

Role of stomach acid -- a step of human digestion, the second clause of C 3.2-LO-1. Not C 1.3 despite the acid: the assessed idea is enzyme activation and germ-killing in the gut, not acid-base chemistry.
DEFECT: stem reads 'junction of digestive enzymes', an OCR corruption of 'function'. The intended question -- what digestive enzymes do -- is a step of human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.

How the small intestine is designed to absorb food -- villi and microvilli increasing surface area. C 4.2-LO-1 names the villus explicitly and is the structure-to-function outcome; C 3.2-LO-1 would be the right code for the chemistry of digestion, but this asks about anatomy serving a function.
Advantage a terrestrial organism has over an aquatic one in obtaining oxygen. A cross-organism comparison of respiration, so the competency C 3.2, not LO-2, which is restricted to the human pathway.
How oxygen and carbon dioxide are transported in human beings -- haemoglobin and plasma, named organs and tissues. Squarely C 3.2-LO-2.
How lungs maximise the area for gas exchange -- the alveolus, named in C 4.2-LO-1. Chosen over C 3.2-LO-2 because the question is about the structure achieving the function, not the pathway of air.

Components of the human transport system and their functions (heart, blood vessels, blood, lymph). Naming the organs of transport is C 3.2-LO-2. Stem says 'junctions' where it means 'functions' -- same OCR fault as qid:85601.
Why oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept apart in birds and mammals -- the double-circulation argument, part of the transport pathway in C 3.2-LO-2.

Components of the transport system in highly organised PLANTS -- xylem and phloem, which is C 4.3-LO-1. Deliberately not C 3.2-LO-2, the human-transport outcome, although the question is worded almost identically to qid:85606.
How water and minerals move in plants -- root pressure and transpiration pull in the xylem, C 4.3-LO-1.
How food is transported in plants -- translocation in the phloem, the other half of C 4.3-LO-1.

How plants get rid of excretory products (gums, resins, leaf fall, release into soil). Excretion is inside C 3.2, but LO-2 covers excretion in HUMAN beings only, so the competency is the correct level here.

How urine volume is regulated -- selective reabsorption in the nephron tubule, part of the human excretory pathway in C 3.2-LO-2. Not C 4.2-LO-1: the question is about regulation, not about nephron structure serving a function.
Kidneys belong to the system for excretion -- placing an organ in its life process, C 3.2-LO-2. (Marks field says 5 for a one-line MCQ; see the defect list.)
Xylem transports water -- the plant-transport outcome C 4.3-LO-1, not the human one.
Autotrophic nutrition requires CO2, water, chlorophyll and light -- the autotrophic clause of C 3.2-LO-1.

Where pyruvate is broken down to CO2, water and energy. The question asks for the ORGANELLE, and C 3.1 is the competency about what cell organelles including mitochondria do. C 3.2-LO-3 would be right if it asked about products or energy yield, but it asks about location.
How and where fats are digested -- bile emulsification then lipase in the small intestine, a step of human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
Role of saliva in digestion -- salivary amylase acting on starch, C 3.2-LO-1.
Conditions and by-products of autotrophic nutrition -- C 3.2-LO-1's autotrophic clause.

Differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration plus organisms that respire anaerobically. This is the whole of C 3.2-LO-3 (products and energy released); LO-2 is about the respiratory pathway and organs, which is not what is asked.
How alveoli are designed to maximise gas exchange -- thin walls, capillary network, huge surface area. C 4.2-LO-1 names the alveolus.
Consequence of haemoglobin deficiency -- impaired oxygen transport, C 3.2-LO-2.
Describe double circulation and why it is necessary -- the human circulatory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
Differences between xylem and phloem transport -- C 4.3-LO-1, which is exactly the xylem/phloem contrast.
Compare alveoli and nephrons in structure and functioning. C 4.2-LO-1 is the only outcome that names both, and the question is explicitly a structure-to-function comparison.

Two functions of the leaf epidermis -- protection and, through its stomata, gas exchange and transpiration control. C 3.2 covers exchange of materials; C 3.1 is reserved here for questions about the guard cell's own water relations, which this is not.

Why only a turgid leaf is chosen for a temporary mount. What is assessed is the experimental choice, not a life process. CG 8 (exploring the nature of Science by doing Science) is cited as a GOAL because its only competency, C 8.1, is about building geometric/mathematical/graphical models -- a microscopy technique is not one, so no competency genuinely fits.
How to remove excess stain from a leaf peel and what happens if cotton wool is used. Pure laboratory technique; same reasoning as qid:85627 for citing the goal rather than C 8.1.

Stem is 'What does the diagram depict?' with no printed figure, but the stored model answer says gaseous exchange in Amoeba. Exchange of materials across a unicellular body surface -- the competency C 3.2, since LO-2 is human-specific.
Figure-dependent stem, resolved by the stored answer: double circulation, with A pulmonary and B systemic. Human transport pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.

How viruses can be called living when they show no movement. The assessed idea is the criteria for life -- molecular movement -- so the competency C 3.2, the same code as qid:85595, which asks the question directly.

Defines the primary reaction of photosynthesis and the Calvin cycle (autotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1) alongside the Krebs cycle, EMP and oxidative phosphorylation (respiratory pathways and energy release, C 3.2-LO-3). Both cited because the item straddles the two.
Why a widely girdled tree dies -- the phloem ring is removed and translocation stops. C 4.3-LO-1, the phloem half of plant transport.

Figure item resolved by the stored answer: A is the stomatal pore and B the guard cell, with a function for each -- guard cells open the pore when turgid and close it when flaccid. That turgor mechanism is cell-level water movement, C 3.1.

Why the uncovered part of the leaf turns blue-black with iodine in the light-is-essential experiment. The content is starch from photosynthesis (C 3.2-LO-1); the reasoning is reading a controlled variable off an experimental result, which is C 8.1's 'manipulate variables and predict results'.
Why multicellular organisms need special gas-exchange organs. Same body-organisation argument as qid:85594, so the same code C 4.2, not a respiration LO.

The green dots in a leaf peel are chloroplasts and the colour is chlorophyll. C 3.1 names the chloroplast among the cellular components; the question is about the organelle, not about photosynthesis as a process.
Breakdown of glucose in the presence and absence of oxygen -- the aerobic/anaerobic comparison, C 3.2-LO-3.
Digestion in mouth, stomach and small intestine -- the steps of nutrition in human beings, C 3.2-LO-1.

Six one-word answers. Photosynthesis, autotrophs, heterotrophs and pepsin are nutrition (C 3.2-LO-1); guard cells and the chloroplast are cellular components (C 3.1). Both cited because neither covers more than half the item.

Whether plants really give out only oxygen by day and only CO2 by night. The answer requires holding photosynthesis and respiration together and comparing their rates, which is the competency C 3.2 rather than the autotrophic-only LO-1 or the aerobic/anaerobic LO-3.
How guard cells regulate the stomatal pore -- water entering and leaving the guard cell changes its turgor. This is the semi-permeable-membrane strand of C 3.1, not a gas-exchange question.

Two plants in oxygen-free containers, one dark and one lit -- which lives longer. The biology is that photosynthesis supplies the oxygen respiration needs, so the competency C 3.2 covering both processes; the light/dark contrast is a controlled-variable prediction, C 8.1.
Does daytime CO2 release mean photosynthesis has stopped? Again the net effect of two simultaneous processes, so C 3.2 rather than either single-process LO.
Why fishes die out of water -- gills collapse and cannot exchange gases in air. A non-human respiration question, so the competency C 3.2, not LO-2.
Differentiate autotroph from heterotroph -- the first clause of C 3.2-LO-1, mapped identically to qid:85598 because the frame offers nothing finer than that one outcome.
